_comment: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT REAL. Every value here is invented, unlike piper-desktop.json which is a real case. This example exists because six consecutive investigations in this format all returned TP-High, so the format had never been made to say 'this is fine' — which is the more common real-world outcome by a wide margin. It also shows the shape of a short report: a thin investigation should produce a short document, not a padded one.
answer: The RPC reconnaissance from this host is its CI agent enumerating its own build fleet on a five-minute schedule, and the pattern is identical on the four other agents in the same group.
next_action: No containment. Recommend a triage rule scoped to the `ci-build-agents` group for detection type `Suspicious Remote Execution`, so the next 288 daily occurrences do not reach the queue. Do **not** scope the rule by detection type alone — the same type from outside this group is exactly what you want to keep seeing.
composition: Both detections score `threat 25 / certainty 30` and the entity sits at urgency 41 — low enough that this would ordinarily be left in the queue rather than resolved. That is the argument for closing it properly: an unexplained low-urgency entity firing 288 times a day is what trains an analyst to ignore the queue.

timeline.title: Targeted RPC reconnaissance
timeline.detail: `LsarLookupNames4` against the four peer agents. First seen 2026-06-02, still firing. `first_timestamp` to `last_timestamp` spans 93 days.

timeline.title: Suspicious remote execution
timeline.detail: `svcctl` service query — not `StartServiceW`. Reads state, starts nothing. Account `svc_ci_agent`, privilege 2.

established.claim: The behaviour predates any incident window and never changes.
established.evidence: Detection 20411 has fired continuously since 2026-06-02 with 11 seconds of drift across 93 days. A schedule, not a person — and nothing about it has escalated in three months.

established.claim: All five agents in the group behave identically.
established.evidence: The same detection type, the same target set, the same interval on `build-agent-05` through `build-agent-09`. A compromise that reproduced itself this precisely across five hosts and then did nothing else for 93 days is not a plausible reading.

established.claim: The account is purpose-scoped and has not been used elsewhere.
established.evidence: `svc_ci_agent` appears in access history on the five agents and the orchestrator only. No interactive logon, no cloud surface, privilege 2 throughout.

sweep.claim: Nothing left the estate, and that is a proven negative rather than an absence of evidence.
sweep.evidence: An Investigation Query for outbound sessions from 10.20.44.19 over 14 days returned only the internal 10.20.44.0/24 range and the OS update endpoints. **Control query**: the same table without the host predicate returned 4.1 million rows for the window, so the feed is populated and the empty result means what it says.

gaps.question: Is this really the CI agent, or something wearing its account?
gaps.detail: The orchestrator's own scheduled task list, retrieved by the asset owner, matches the interval and target set exactly. Confirmed by a human who owns the system, not inferred from timing.

gaps.question: Do the peer agents show the same pattern, or is this host the odd one out?
gaps.detail: One entity listing filtered to the group. All five identical. Had this host been the only one, the verdict would have gone the other way.

next_steps.title: Write the triage rule scoped to the group, then re-check in 30 days
next_steps.why: A rule scoped too broadly hides the same behaviour arriving from somewhere that matters. Re-checking is how you find out it was scoped too broadly.

evidence.what: svcctl service query only — no service creation or start
No egress; control query proves the table is populated
Orchestrator scheduled task matches interval and targets
